title: Rossi Street to Lincoln Center: the Ballet Master Who Built the Room
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The School He Did Not Want

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the birth in the imperial capital
stops.date_confidence: attested; 9 January by the Julian calendar still in use in Russia, 22 January by the Gregorian
stops.campa: Georgiy Melitonovich Balanchivadze is born in the imperial capital on the ninth of January by the old calendar, the twenty-second by the new. His father Meliton is a Georgian composer; his mother Maria Nikolayevna Vasilyeva keeps the house. The street is not recorded in any standard biography. Music is the family trade. Nobody in the household is preparing a dancer. Within nine years the boy will be delivered across town to a school he does not want, and the surname will begin its long shortening toward a Western marquee.
suggested_refs: The Balanchivadze household in Saint Petersburg; Meliton Balanchivadze's Georgian songbooks
sources: Bernard Taper, Balanchine: A Biography (1984), at second hand

stops.name: Karelian Isthmus, the summers before the Revolution
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pool dated it c.1910-1913 and named Lounatjoki while pinning a point 40 km away, so the pin is moved to Lounatjoki and the place named generically
stops.campa: Summers before the Revolution are spent at a rented dacha on the pine coast running north toward Finland, along the Vyborg rail line. Biographers place the family among birch groves and lake light, and the boy performs for relatives in amateur theatricals on the veranda. No address survives. The isthmus becomes foreign ground once the Treaty of Tartu fixes the border in 1920, and he never sees it again. It is the last landscape of his life that schools and states have not yet arranged for him.
suggested_refs: The pre-revolutionary dacha belt of the Karelian Isthmus, Vyborg line
sources: Taper, Balanchine (anecdotal chapters), at second hand
Solomon Volkov, Balanchine's Tchaikovsky (interviews), at second hand

stops.name: Imperial Theatre School, Rossi Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1913; the pool fixes no month, and the pin is corrected to the Vaganova Academy's own coordinate at 2 Rossi Street
stops.campa: At nine he is deposited at the Imperial Theatre School on Rossi Street, enrolled at his mother's insistence, and he cries through the entrance audition. The street is one of the most exactly proportioned in Europe, laid out by Carlo Rossi in a single unbroken axis of yellow classical facades. He boards here and is drilled daily in the Petipa vocabulary Russia has spent a century perfecting, under Pavel Gerdt and Samuil Andrianov. Eight years earlier Isadora Duncan danced barefoot in this city before Diaghilev, Fokine and Pavlova.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Theatre School, 2 Rossi Street, now the Vaganova Academy of Russian Ballet

stops.name: Petrograd, the first choreography: La Nuit
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1920; no venue and no day are fixed by the sources, and the school is used as the pin because the earliest pieces were shown at student concerts
stops.campa: At sixteen he makes his first piece of choreography, a pas de deux called La Nuit set to music by Anton Rubinstein, shown at a student concert rather than on any state stage. The same year he is said to try a version of Cocteau and Milhaud's Le Boeuf sur le toit for experimental staging in Petrograd, a claim the record carries much more thinly. The school teaches the classical canon and he is already outside it. The directorate asked for neither piece and approves of neither.
suggested_refs: La Nuit, pas de deux to Anton Rubinstein, Petrograd 1920, the first Balanchine work

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, the corps de ballet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of graduation, 1921; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: He graduates and joins the corps of the state theatre built as the Mariinsky, renamed after the Revolution and still standing on Theatre Square in its turquoise paint. He dances the standard repertory through real cold and real hunger, the imperial subsidy gone and the Bolshevik one unreliable. This is Petipa's house: The Sleeping Beauty opened here in 1890 and The Nutcracker in 1892, both to Tchaikovsky's scores. Thirty-three years from now, in another country, he will make his own Nutcracker out of this memory.
suggested_refs: The former Mariinsky, Theatre Square, Petrograd, under the early Soviet administration

stops.name: Petrograd Conservatory, the composer's ear
stops.date_confidence: attested to the enrolment years 1921-1923; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: Alongside the corps work he enrolls at the conservatory Anton Rubinstein founded, a short walk from the Mariinsky stage door, and studies piano, theory, counterpoint, harmony and composition. He learns to read a score the way other choreographers read a libretto. Later accounts of why his ballets fit the note as closely as the step point back to this building rather than to any studio. He graduates in 1923: a dancer with a composer's training and no company willing to use it.
suggested_refs: The Petrograd Conservatory, founded by Anton Rubinstein, near Theatre Square

stops.name: Petrograd, the marriage to Tamara Geva
stops.date_confidence: contested and not adjudicated: the Wikipedia Balanchine infobox says 1921, the Wikipedia Tamara Geva article says 1924, Taper says 1922; Geva was born 17 March 1906, making her 15, 18 and 16 respectively. 1922 is used only as the middle reading
stops.campa: He marries the dancer Tamara Geva in the city of his birth. The year is not settled: one source says 1921, another 1924, a third 1922, and Geva was born in March 1906, which makes her fifteen, eighteen or sixteen depending on which is right. Every account agrees the marriage is quick and that it does not survive long past the border. She becomes one of the four, with Alexandra Danilova and Nicholas Efimov, who leave the country together under a state contract meant to be temporary. The divorce comes in 1926.
suggested_refs: The three irreconcilable marriage dates for Balanchine and Tamara Geva

stops.name: Mikhailovsky Theatre, Evenings of the Young Ballet
stops.date_confidence: the ensemble is attested to 1923; the Mikhailovsky venue is reconstruction, since the Wikipedia article cited for it does not mention the theatre at all
stops.campa: With Tamara Geva and other young dancers he forms an ensemble called Evenings of the Young Ballet and takes it onto the smaller Petrograd stages, the Mikhailovsky among them, a hall built for the imperial family's private amusement and now absorbed into the state system. The programs set Petipa variations beside experiments the Mariinsky's senior staff will not sanction. It is a cheap enough place to fail in. The senior staff notice anyway, and the pressure on him to stop begins here.
suggested_refs: Programs of the Evenings of the Young Ballet, Petrograd 1923
sources: Wikipedia, 'George Balanchine' (ensemble only; the venue is not in the article)

stops.name: Stettin, the first foreign soil
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the summer 1924 crossing is Taper's route reconstruction and the month is not documented
stops.campa: The four dancers, billed as the Soviet State Dancers and later as the Young Ballet, cross into Germany at the Baltic port of Stettin on a contract permitting them to tour abroad for hard currency. It is the first foreign soil of Balanchine's life. Biographers disagree over the details of the crossing; the port itself, German then and Polish Szczecin now, is the one fixed marker. None of the four will live under Soviet rule again, and none of them knows that yet.
suggested_refs: The 1924 Soviet touring contract that let four dancers out and was never honoured in reverse
sources: Taper, Balanchine (route reconstruction), at second hand
General Ballets Russes historiography of the 1924 departure

stops.name: Berlin, the program nobody wants
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924; the day is a placement within the reconstructed summer route
stops.campa: The quartet reaches Berlin and is received badly. The city's cabaret and concert audiences are unmoved by a program improvised out of conservatory pieces and salvaged Mariinsky variations, and the money runs out fast. Berlin is the capital of a defeated republic still recovering from its own currency, and it offers no rescue. Thirty-three years later Mary Wigman will stage her last major work in this city to Stravinsky's Sacre, the composer whose score is about to make Balanchine's name. The four move on rather than starve.
suggested_refs: The Young Ballet's Berlin program, summer 1924

stops.name: Wiesbaden, the spa circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924; the day is a placement within the reconstructed summer route
stops.campa: Failing in Berlin, the troupe retreats to the German spa towns and takes what a resort circuit built for older, wealthier clientele will offer. Wiesbaden's casino theatres and summer gardens book them, and then Bad Ems in the Rhine Province does the same. Geva recalls it without sentiment: dark rooms, small houses, meals skipped more often than eaten, and on one night an audience of mental patients. The engagements pay just enough to keep the group moving west toward London.
suggested_refs: The Rhineland spa theatres of Wiesbaden and Bad Ems, summer 1924

stops.name: London, two weeks of dead silence
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924; the month is a placement within the reconstructed route
stops.campa: In London the Young Ballet plays a two-week engagement and meets, in Geva's word, dead silence. The houses are polite and nothing follows: no bookings, no press worth quoting. Their Soviet travel documents are close to expiring and England has no appetite for four unknown Russians performing salvaged classical variations. The failure forces the decision. Rather than return to a state increasingly hostile to artists who have seen the outside, they choose Paris and the uncertain protection of the emigres already there.
suggested_refs: The Young Ballet's unreviewed London fortnight, autumn 1924

stops.name: Paris, the Russian quarter on the rue Daru
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1924; the pin is corrected to the Cathedral of Saint Alexander Nevsky at 12 rue Daru, the pool's figure having fallen near Place des Ternes
stops.campa: They settle among the tens of thousands of Russians who fled the Revolution into Paris, many of them clustered around the gold-domed cathedral of Saint Alexander Nevsky on the rue Daru, a parish that works as labour exchange and news bureau as much as church. Balanchine, Geva, Danilova and Efimov arrive with no contract and expiring papers, indistinguishable at first from thousands of others: officers driving taxis, dancers waiting tables. Paris is where the improvised tour finally pays.
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of Saint Alexander Nevsky, 12 rue Daru, hub of emigre Paris

stops.name: Paris, the audition and the shortened name
stops.date_confidence: the hiring and the renaming are attested; November 1924 is the standard dating and the day is not documented
stops.campa: Sergei Diaghilev, rebuilding the Ballets Russes after a decade of reinventions, auditions the Soviet arrivals and hires Balanchine at once, first as a dancer and almost immediately as a choreographer. Within weeks the impresario has shortened Balanchivadze to Balanchine, the name every later contract will carry. Diaghilev has been circling this world for years: Suzanne Perrottet's Hellerau festival of 1912 counted him among its visitors. A twenty-year-old refugee with no Western reputation is inside the most famous ballet company in Europe within a season of arriving.
suggested_refs: Diaghilev's 1924 contracts with the four Soviet State Dancers

stops.name: Salle Garnier, Monte Carlo: chief choreographer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the promotion year 1925 and the winter seasons 1925-1929; no day is fixed
stops.campa: Every winter the Ballets Russes decamps to Monte Carlo and works in the small gilt Salle Garnier that Charles Garnier built onto the casino. Made chief choreographer in 1925, after Diaghilev tires of Bronislava Nijinska, Balanchine sets some ten new ballets here across the company's final seasons, rehearsing through the Mediterranean off-season and touring the results across Europe. He works with Prokofiev, Stravinsky, Satie and Ravel, and with Picasso, Rouault and Matisse. A principality living on gambling revenue houses the workshop of neoclassical ballet.
suggested_refs: The Salle Garnier of the Casino de Monte-Carlo, winter home of the Ballets Russes

stops.name: London, the kneecap and the end of dancing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the city and the outcome are in the biographies, the pitch is unrecorded and accounts differ on the year, c.1927 used here
stops.campa: During one of the company's London seasons he joins other dancers in an informal football match and shatters his kneecap. The injury ends any prospect of a major performing career and pushes him, not yet twenty-five, into choreography as his only professional identity. The standard sources record the city and the outcome, not the pitch or the day, and they disagree about the year. At the time it is simply an injury that keeps a young company member off the stage for months.
suggested_refs: The undocumented London football match that ended Balanchine's dancing
sources: General Ballets Russes biography; date and place vary across accounts

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, Paris: Apollon musagete
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Apollon musagete, set to Stravinsky's score for strings, is given with the Ballets Russes at the Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt beside the Place du Chatelet. He strips the ornament away and leaves the structure exposed. The stage is built out of line rather than pantomime. Diaghilev, watching the final rehearsal, is reported to recognize a new language rather than a variation on Fokine or Nijinska. The ballet outlives the company that made it by more than half a century, and Balanchine will name it as the hinge of everything that follows.
stops.quote: Apollo I look back on as the turning point of my life.
stops.quote_source: Balanchine, in Walter Sorell (ed.), The Dance Has Many Faces; the same wording in Don McDonagh, George Balanchine, and in Lincoln Kirstein, Program Notes. Wikipedia's variant 'the turning point in my life,' cited to an unresolvable 'Fisher (2006), p. 27,' is a misquotation
suggested_refs: Apollon musagete, Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, 12 June 1928, Stravinsky and Balanchine's first collaboration
sources: Open Library search-inside: McDonagh, Kirstein, Sorell

stops.name: London Coliseum, the variety years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1929-1933; the month is a placement after Diaghilev's death in August 1929
stops.campa: Diaghilev dies in August, four months after The Prodigal Son opened to Prokofiev's score, and the Ballets Russes goes bankrupt within the year. Balanchine takes work in London for the producers Charles B. Cochran and Oswald Stoll, staging dances at the Coliseum on St Martin's Lane, a cavernous variety house built for spectacle. Revues and musical numbers replace symphonic ballets. The work is commercial and it keeps him employed through the four years between one great company's death and the arrival of the next patron.
suggested_refs: Cochran's revues and Stoll's variety bills at the London Coliseum, 1929-1933

stops.name: Royal Danish Theatre, Copenhagen: guest ballet master
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1930; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: He spends part of the year as guest ballet master at the Royal Danish Theatre, one of the oldest continuously operating ballet companies in Europe and still built around the nineteenth-century Bournonville style. The engagement is brief and leaves almost no trace in his own later account of himself. The Danish company's preserved repertory and its discipline sit oddly beside the revue work he is doing in London in the same months. He is a choreographer of the first rank with no company of his own.
suggested_refs: The Bournonville repertory of the Royal Danish Ballet, kept intact since the 1830s

stops.name: Salle Garnier, Monte Carlo: the baby ballerinas
stops.date_confidence: 1932, not the 1931 given by one lens of the research pool: the Ballets Russes de Monte-Carlo was founded in 1932 by Rene Blum and Colonel Wassily de Basil, and Serge Denham, named in that lens, headed a rival company only from 1938
stops.campa: The Ballets Russes name and much of its personnel regroup as the Ballets Russes de Monte-Carlo under Rene Blum and Colonel Wassily de Basil, and Balanchine returns to the same stage as founding choreographer. He makes Cotillon and La Concurrence for a new generation, the teenaged Tamara Toumanova, Irina Baronova and Tatiana Riabouchinska among them, and works alongside Leonide Massine. Within about a year artistic disputes push him out, back into the freelance uncertainty that has held since Diaghilev died.
suggested_refs: Cotillon and La Concurrence, Monte Carlo 1932, and the three baby ballerinas

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees, Paris: Les Ballets 1933
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1933; the pool fixes no day
stops.campa: He forms his own company, Les Ballets 1933, with Boris Kochno and money from the English poet and eccentric Edward James, and opens on the avenue Montaigne with Mozartiana and The Seven Deadly Sins, made with Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht around Lotte Lenya. This is the hall where the Rite of Spring came apart in 1913, the premiere Marcel Proust is reported to have attended, and where Gurdjieff's pupils gave their movements demonstrations in December 1923. The company folds within months for lack of money.
suggested_refs: Les Ballets 1933 at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees, 15 avenue Montaigne

stops.name: Savoy Theatre, London: Kirstein in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1933; the pool fixes no day
stops.campa: Les Ballets 1933 crosses to London for a short season, and in the audience sits Lincoln Kirstein, a young American writer and heir with an unfashionable ambition: an American ballet company built out of an American school rather than imported Russian stars. Kirstein approaches him after a performance with an invitation to New York. Balanchine has no functioning company and Europe is closing around independent ventures. He accepts, and the nine years of borrowed companies since Stettin come to an end.
suggested_refs: Lincoln Kirstein's London approach, July 1933, and the letters that followed
sources: Kirstein biography and New York City Ballet historiography

stops.name: New York Harbor, arrival aboard the SS Olympic
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He sails from Europe aboard the SS Olympic and lands in New York in October, met at the pier by Kirstein and Edward Warburg, the two young men bankrolling the venture. He arrives with almost no English, a small circle of emigre collaborators, and a plan that exists mostly on paper. Nothing about the port marks the moment. It is the last border he crosses as an itinerant, and every move he makes for the next fifty years will begin from an American address.
suggested_refs: Passenger records of the SS Olympic, October 1933
sources: New York City Ballet institutional history

stops.name: 637 Madison Avenue, the School of American Ballet opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, with the address and the 32-student figure; the pin is corrected to 637 Madison Avenue at East 59th Street, both pool figures having been wrong
stops.campa: The School of American Ballet opens at 637 Madison Avenue on the second of January with thirty-two students and no company waiting to absorb them. Kirstein had wanted a company directly. Balanchine insists on the school first, on the ground that no American dancer yet exists trained to the standard his choreography will require. The insistence sets the pattern of the rest of his working life: build the institution, then make the work the institution can hold. The school is still open.
stops.quote_source: Reported as Balanchine's answer to Lincoln Kirstein on arriving in America, 1933. The George Balanchine Foundation's own biography page hedges it as 'famously reported to have said'; no primary transcript has been located, so this is tradition rather than verified quotation
suggested_refs: The School of American Ballet's first premises, 637 Madison Avenue at East 59th Street

stops.name: Woodlands, White Plains: Serenade on the lawn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the lawn of Woodlands, the Warburg family's estate north of the city, his students give the first performance of Serenade, set to Tchaikovsky's Serenade for Strings, danced outdoors at dusk before an invited audience. A rehearsal accident, a dancer falling and another arriving late, is folded permanently into the finished choreography rather than corrected out. It is the first ballet he makes in America and becomes one of the most performed works of the century. Its stage that night is somebody's lawn.
suggested_refs: Serenade, first danced at the Warburg estate, 10 June 1934
sources: New York City Ballet repertory notes on Serenade

stops.name: Avery Memorial, Hartford: the first public performance
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the venue; the performers were billed as the Producing Company of the School of American Ballet, not as the American Ballet, whose own debut was 1 March 1935 at the Adelphi Theatre in New York
stops.campa: Balanchine's American students give their first public performance not in New York but in Hartford, at the Avery Memorial theatre of the Wadsworth Atheneum, whose director A. Everett Austin has cultivated exactly the avant-garde patronage the project needs. They are billed as the Producing Company of the School of American Ballet. The choice of a provincial museum theatre over a Broadway house measures how uncertain the venture still is eleven months after the school opened.
suggested_refs: The Avery Memorial wing of the Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford, under A. Everett Austin

stops.name: Metropolitan Opera House, the uneasy residency
stops.date_confidence: attested to the residency period 1935-1938; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: The American Ballet becomes resident company of the Metropolitan Opera House, an arrangement meant to give the dancers a major stage and steady wages. It is uneasy from the start. Met management wants dances for operas and Balanchine wants to make independent symphonic ballets. After a badly received season of new commissions in 1936 the residency is not renewed. In the same years he choreographs On Your Toes for Rodgers and Hart, the first Broadway show billed as choreography by him rather than as dances staged.
stops.quote: If only you would learn to do battement tendu properly you wouldn't have to learn anything else.
stops.quote_source: Balanchine in the studio, quoted in Maria Tallchief with Larry Kaplan, Maria Tallchief: America's Prima Ballerina (Henry Holt, 1998), ch. 3; reached through the Wikipedia article 'Maria Tallchief', the memoir text not examined directly
suggested_refs: On Your Toes (1936), with La Princesse Zenobia and Slaughter on Tenth Avenue

stops.name: North Fairfax Avenue, Hollywood: the film years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1938; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: He relocates to Hollywood, renting a house on North Fairfax Avenue with the rehearsal pianist Nicholas Kopeikine, and builds dance sequences for Samuel Goldwyn. On the set of The Goldwyn Follies he meets the dancer Vera Zorina and marries her the same year. It is the only extended period he spends away from New York after 1933, working inside a system that treats dance as an interlude between the parts of a film that matter. He does not stay. By the mid-1940s he is back in New York.
suggested_refs: The Goldwyn Follies (1938) and the Zorina dance sequences

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, the dancers sent to Joseph Pilates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1941 in joseph_pilates.journey.json, which corrected an impossible 1931 date on the ground that Balanchine did not reach the United States until October 1933
stops.campa: He begins sending injured dancers to Joseph Pilates, whose gymnasium sits at 939 Eighth Avenue in a building that also holds dance schools and rehearsal rooms. Romana Kryzanowska of the School of American Ballet is among them. The German boxer and inventor, interned on the Isle of Man in one war and rebuilding bodies in another country by the next, becomes the man Balanchine's company trusts with its knees and its backs. The arrangement outlives them both.
suggested_refs: The Pilates gymnasium at 939 Eighth Avenue and its dance-school neighbours

stops.name: Teatro Colon, Buenos Aires: the Good Neighbor tour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1941 South American tour is documented, the venue-level itinerary is not independently reverified and no month is fixed
stops.campa: Under a State Department Good Neighbor program, Kirstein and Balanchine send American Ballet Caravan south, and the company plays the Teatro Colon in Buenos Aires among other houses. The tour is wartime soft power aimed at a region Washington fears is drifting toward the Axis, an odd diplomatic errand for a company five years old. Five years earlier Victoria Ocampo stood on this same stage speaking the title role in Stravinsky's Persephone, having housed the composer and his son before the premiere.
suggested_refs: American Ballet Caravan's 1941 South American itinerary under the Office of Inter-American Affairs
sources: Lincoln Kirstein's writings and American Ballet Caravan historiography

stops.name: Theatro Municipal, Rio de Janeiro: the Caravan folds
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; this stop is not independently reverified and the month is a placement inside the 1941 tour. The pool gave a positive latitude, which plots in the North Atlantic; the sign is corrected here
stops.campa: The Caravan continues to Rio de Janeiro and the Theatro Municipal, a Belle Epoque house modelled deliberately on the Paris Opera. Reception across the tour is mixed. Some audiences take to the unfamiliar neoclassical repertory; others expect the story ballets still touring the hemisphere under the Ballets Russes name and find plotless abstraction puzzling. The tour loses money and the company folds not long after it returns north. He has not yet held an ensemble together for longer than a few seasons.
suggested_refs: The Theatro Municipal do Rio de Janeiro, Praca Floriano
sources: Wikipedia, 'Theatro Municipal (Rio de Janeiro)' for the coordinate

stops.name: New York, Ballet Society and The Four Temperaments
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the venue is not. Ballet Society's first seasons were not given at City Center, but the research pool fixes no hall, so the City Center pin stands as an approximation and the gap is stated
stops.campa: With Kirstein he forms Ballet Society, a subscription company answerable to a few hundred members rather than to a box office, and on the twentieth of November it gives The Four Temperaments to a score commissioned from Paul Hindemith. The ballet is spare and without plot. He marries Maria Tallchief the same year. In 1948 he makes Orpheus with Stravinsky and the sculptor Isamu Noguchi, and the subscription experiment turns out to have been a company all along.
stops.quote: Maria, I would like you to become my wife.
stops.quote_source: Balanchine to Maria Tallchief, quoted in Maria Tallchief with Larry Kaplan, Maria Tallchief: America's Prima Ballerina (Henry Holt, 1998), ch. 3; reached through the Wikipedia article 'Maria Tallchief', the memoir text not examined directly
suggested_refs: Hindemith's commissioned score for The Four Temperaments, premiered 20 November 1946

stops.name: New York City Center, the company gets its name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1948; the pool fixes no month. The two lenses of the pool give City Center as 40.7648/-73.9808 and 40.7639/-73.9794, about 150 m apart, and the disagreement is not adjudicated
stops.campa: Ballet Society is invited to become resident company of the New York City Center of Music and Drama on West 55th Street and is renamed New York City Ballet. The building is a converted Shriners' temple with a Moorish-revival dome, nothing like an opera house. From this stage, over the next sixteen years, he builds ballet by ballet the repertory that will define American classical dance. He has founded or co-founded five companies since 1933. This is the one that holds.
stops.quote: The only justification I have is to enable Balanchine to do exactly what he wants to do in the way he wants to do it.
stops.quote_source: Lincoln Kirstein, letter of 1946, quoted via Alastair Macaulay's review of Martin Duberman, The Worlds of Lincoln Kirstein, The New York Times, 4 May 2007
suggested_refs: The Mecca Temple on West 55th Street, converted into New York City Center

stops.name: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden: the London debut
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1950 in touring historiography; no month is fixed and no primary programme was consulted
stops.campa: New York City Ballet makes its London debut at Covent Garden, the first major European exposure for a company two years old. The London critical establishment, formed on the Royal Ballet's narrative and decorative tradition under Ninette de Valois, reacts with some hostility to the stripped abstraction and reads Maria Tallchief's technical brilliance as coldness. The company leaves recognized abroad for the first time as a rival tradition rather than a provincial offshoot. Edinburgh follows in the early fifties.
stops.quote: I always thought Balanchine was more of a musician even than a choreographer, and perhaps that's why he and I connected.
stops.quote_source: Maria Tallchief, 'Maria Tallchief: Lithe, Fantastic,' The Washington Post, 8 December 1996. Wikipedia attributes these words to Sarah Halzack's 2013 obituary; the phone-interview framing of the 1996 profile shows they predate it by seventeen years
suggested_refs: The 1950 Covent Garden season and its hostile London notices
sources: New York City Ballet touring historiography
General ballet criticism of the period

stops.name: New York City Center, the Nutcracker becomes an institution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1954; the research pool fixes no day
stops.campa: He makes his own Nutcracker for New York City Ballet, to the score first heard at the Mariinsky in December 1892, and dances the mime role of Drosselmeyer himself. Tchaikovsky's ballet was judged a slight thing at its premiere and the composer died eleven months later without knowing otherwise. In Balanchine's version it becomes an annual Christmas fixture that pays the company's bills, and then the model other American companies copy. He married Tanaquil LeClercq two years before, the last of his dancer wives.
suggested_refs: Balanchine's Nutcracker, New York City Ballet, 1954, danced with the choreographer as Drosselmeyer

stops.name: Weston, Connecticut: the country house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool dates the tenancy loosely to the 1940s-1983 and notes that the exact address and years differ across sources, so the date here is a placement only
stops.campa: For much of his American life he keeps a country place in the wooded exurb of Weston, where he gardens, cooks the Georgian dishes he learned at his father's table, and leaves the city between seasons. The house appears rarely in the official record; it is where he is not working. Colleagues describe an almost monastic domestic routine there, nothing like the rehearsal-room tyrant of the memoirs. The exact address and the years of tenancy differ between accounts and are not settled.
suggested_refs: Dancer memoirs describing the Weston house and its kitchen
sources: New York City Ballet dancer memoirs; address and years uncertain

stops.name: Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow: the defector comes back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; October 1962 is the standard dating of the Soviet tour's Moscow leg and no day is fixed in the reachable accounts
stops.campa: New York City Ballet performs in Moscow under a Cold War cultural exchange, and Balanchine sets foot in his own country for the first time since he left it at twenty. Soviet critics trained on narrative Bolshoi drama call the work formalist and cold; audiences reportedly give sustained ovations anyway. He gives interviews carefully, aware that every word passes through a state that still files him as a defector rather than as a returning son. He has been an American citizen for two decades.
suggested_refs: The 1962 US-Soviet cultural exchange agreement under which the company toured

stops.name: Kirov Theatre, Leningrad: the stage he trained on
stops.date_confidence: attested to the October-November 1962 leg; no day is fixed
stops.campa: The tour reaches Leningrad and the company plays the Kirov, which is the Mariinsky under a Soviet name, the stage where he trained and first danced under the tsars. He is reported visibly moved on re-entering the building after thirty-eight years and gives little away in public. Former teachers and classmates, some still living, come to the performances. The reunion is recorded far more vividly in company members' memoirs than in anything he himself says about it.

stops.name: Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre, the father's country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Tbilisi leg is reported but its extent is not independently reverified and no date is fixed. Fragmentary accounts also add a Kiev stop that nothing reachable confirms
stops.campa: The tour extends to Tbilisi, capital of the country his father came from and which he has never seen. He was born in Saint Petersburg and grew up on Georgian music at Meliton's piano without once setting foot in Georgia. Relatives and cultural officials receive the company as though a lost native son had come home. How much time he spends with family here, and what he says about the connection, varies between accounts and does not reconcile. A monument here will be dedicated to him after his death.
stops.quote: They are my people... I am Georgian myself.
stops.quote_source: Quoted by Anna Kisselgoff, '80 Guests From Balanchine Country,' The New York Times, 2 December 1974
suggested_refs: The monument to Balanchine at the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre

segments.name: Lincoln Center and the Last Illness

stops.name: New York State Theater, the room built to his measurements
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1964; the pool fixes no month
stops.campa: The company moves to the New York State Theater at Lincoln Center, a building Philip Johnson designs in direct consultation with Balanchine, who specifies stage depth, sightlines and a shallow rake suited to how he wants dancers seen. A choreographer is given authorship over the room his work will live in. The company has spent sixteen years in a converted temple. The theatre, renamed for David H. Koch, is still the company's house decades after the architect and the choreographer are both gone.
stops.quote: The ballet is a purely female thing; it is a woman, a garden of beautiful flowers, and man is the gardener.
stops.quote_source: George Balanchine, 'To Get into the Act,' Life, 11 June 1965, p. 97, the citation given by Douglas Crimp in Before Pictures; the same wording is printed in Suki Schorer on the Balanchine Technique and in Simpson's Contemporary Quotations
suggested_refs: Philip Johnson's New York State Theater, designed with Balanchine on stage depth and rake

stops.name: New York State Theater, Jewels
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1967; the research pool fixes no day
stops.campa: Jewels is given in three parts, Emeralds, Rubies and Diamonds, and is taken afterward as the first full-evening ballet with no story in it. Nothing happens. Three manners of dancing are set side by side and the audience is left to do the comparing. He has been making ballets for forty-seven years by now and is credited, on a figure repeated everywhere and traced to no primary catalogue, with some four hundred and sixty-five of them. France gives him the Legion of Honour eight years later.
stops.quote: When Mr. B was working on a ballet, something would just spill out of his body; he could rarely duplicate it, so I tried to see precisely what he wanted the first time.
stops.quote_source: Suzanne Farrell, interview by Emily Fragos, BOMB Magazine, Fall 2003; reached through the Wikipedia article 'Suzanne Farrell', since BOMB's own page returned HTTP 403
suggested_refs: Jewels (1967) and the disputed count of 465 Balanchine works

stops.name: Roosevelt Hospital, Manhattan: losing his balance
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1978 for the onset of symptoms; no month is fixed. The pool's two lenses give the hospital as 40.7697/-73.9885 and 40.7700/-73.9876, about 90 m apart, and the disagreement is not adjudicated
stops.campa: He begins losing his balance while dancing and rehearsing. Angina follows, then heart bypass surgery, then a decline in equilibrium, eyesight and hearing that no doctor treating him can name. The illness will be identified only after his death, as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. He has spent sixty-five years training bodies to keep their balance. In December of the same year he receives the Kennedy Center Honors in Washington, and Austria decorates him two years later.
suggested_refs: The undiagnosed neurological decline of 1978-1983, identified posthumously as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mount Sinai West' for the hospital coordinate

stops.name: Roosevelt Hospital, Manhattan: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies at Roosevelt Hospital on the thirtieth of April, seventy-nine years old, after four years in which he is largely incapacitated. New York City Ballet rehearses his ballets on schedule across town while he is dying a few miles away. He leaves the works themselves inside a legal structure: the George Balanchine Trust, formed the year he dies, licenses them, and a foundation records surviving dancers coaching the steps so that the choreography is not lost with the bodies that first held it.
suggested_refs: The George Balanchine Trust and the Foundation's Video Archives coaching sessions

stops.name: Oakland Cemetery, Sag Harbor: the Orthodox burial
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1983; no day is fixed, and the pin is corrected to the cemetery's own coordinate after the pool offered two different points, one of them outside the cemetery bounds
stops.campa: A Russian Orthodox rite is read and he is buried at Oakland Cemetery in Sag Harbor, at the eastern end of Long Island, a long way from the Manhattan theatres. Biographers attribute the choice variously to a particular Orthodox priest active there and to the quiet of the place. Alexandra Danilova, who crossed the Baltic with him at Stettin in 1924, is buried later in the same ground. Nothing at the site announces who lies under it, and by most accounts the plainness is deliberate.
suggested_refs: Oakland Cemetery, Sag Harbor, graves of Balanchine and Alexandra Danilova

stops.name: George Balanchine Way, West 63rd Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1990; no day is fixed
stops.campa: The stretch of West 63rd Street between Columbus Avenue and Broadway, alongside the theatre built to his specifications, is renamed George Balanchine Way. He was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom in the year he died. A crater thirty-eight kilometres across in Mercury's Raditladi quadrangle carries his name, its blue rays said to recall the tutus of Serenade, the ballet his first American students danced on a lawn in 1934. His papers are at Harvard, in the Houghton Library.
